::: {.why}
The gap between what you average and what you compound is not a curiosity; it is the reason a strategy can have a positive expected return and lose money, and it is one line of algebra.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Derive the approximate relationship between the geometric mean, the arithmetic mean and the variance, and say when the approximation fails.
- Compute the annual drag for a 15 percent volatility asset and for a 60 percent volatility asset, and say which one that argues against.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Derive it: with log returns approximately normal, the expected log return is the arithmetic mean minus half the variance. Do the second-order Taylor expansion yourself rather than quoting the result, and note exactly which step is the approximation.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Verify it against your four numbers from last night. For each asset, compare the measured geometric mean against arithmetic mean minus half the variance. Report the residual. Then compute the drag at 15, 30 and 60 percent annual volatility and tabulate it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} The consequence, in one paragraph: two assets have the same arithmetic mean return and different volatilities. Say which one you would rather own and prove it with the drag table rather than with an argument about risk aversion.
:::
:::
